title: Flowers for Prairie Avenue
premise: Play a florist's delivery runner on a spring morning in 1904, carrying the morning's orders to four mansions on Prairie Avenue and deciding the sequence of your route.

opening.text:
JAUNT: FLOWERS FOR PRAIRIE AVENUE. A spring morning in 1904; you are thirteen, employed to deliver flowers for a florist. This morning's basket contains orders for four households on Prairie Avenue, the city's most celebrated residential street, and every bouquet carries a house number on its tag.

The sequence of deliveries is your decision. The houses and the people living in them are historical; the delivery runner is invented.

stops.text: 1800 Prairie Avenue, the Glessner house, at the corner of Eighteenth Street, receives the first bouquet. Now, consider the woman who lives here. Frances Macbeth Glessner has kept a journal since 1879, maintains beehives, and this year established a silversmith's workbench in the basement so that she could craft silver with her own hands. She and her husband John have occupied the house since 1 December 1887. Three bouquets remain, so you must decide: north first, or south?

choices.label: North to 1700
choices.consequence: Begin with the house one block north.

choices.label: South to 1834
choices.consequence: Begin with the house a few doors south.

stops.text: 1700 Prairie, one block north. John and Frances Glessner built this house and its twin at 1706 for their two married children, and their daughter Frances, who married Blewett Lee in 1898, now lives here; the 1904 Blue Book lists the Lee household at this address. Now, a future nobody on this street could predict. Decades from now she will create the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, miniature crime scenes for training in legal medicine that are still in use. Deliver the bouquet, then continue south past Twentieth Street.

1834 Prairie, the Fernando Jones house, a few doors south. Jane Grahame Jones is a longtime and outspoken activist for woman suffrage; the Fernando Jones scrapbook preserves clippings on the Illinois Woman Suffrage Association from 1875. Despite decades of effort, she still cannot vote. In 1913 Illinois will become the first state east of the Mississippi River to give women the right to vote for president. The house will be torn down in 1942. Deliver the bouquet and continue south past Twentieth Street.
stops.narrative: A household campaigning for the vote.

stops.text: 2036 Prairie, the Buckingham house, where the 1904 Blue Book lists Clarence Buckingham. His sister, Kate Sturges Buckingham, is a philanthropist and art patron. In 1927, after his death, she will fund a fountain dedicated to his memory: twice the size of the Latona Basin at Versailles that inspired it, with a major display that sprays water 150 feet into the air. One bouquet remains in the basket.
stops.narrative: South to 2115, or back north to 1608?

choices.label: South to 2115
choices.consequence: A short walk, one block farther.

choices.label: Back north to 1608
choices.consequence: A long walk with the final bouquet.

stops.text: 2115 Prairie, the Kelley-Armour house. The 1904 Blue Book lists Mrs. Philip D. Armour here, and the 1900 census names her Belle O. Armour, born in Ohio. In the coming decades many of the leading Prairie Avenue families will die or relocate to suburbs such as Lake Forest, but she will remain. The district marker records that she was among the street's last residents, dying here in 1927, and her house will be torn down in 1937. The basket is empty, so return to the shop for the afternoon's orders.
stops.narrative: The final house on your route.

stops.text: 1608 Prairie, the Frank household, at the northern end of your route. Henrietta Greenebaum Frank has worked steadily for quality nursing education at the Illinois Training School for Nurses. In 1876 she and her sister Hannah Greenebaum Solomon became the first Jewish members of the prestigious Chicago Woman's Club, and Hannah went on to found the National Council of Jewish Women. The basket is empty, so return to the shop for the afternoon's orders.
stops.narrative: The northern end of your route.

legs.note: South along the west side of the avenue to 1834.
legs.story: Southward first, along the avenue's western side.

legs.note: South along the avenue, past the Glessner house and Twentieth Street, to 2036.
On south and across the avenue to 2115.
All the way back north along the avenue to 1608.

endings.text: North first, then all the way south: four houses, four doors, and not a single bouquet dropped. The florist says you mastered the avenue in a single morning, and next week the route will be yours to plan.
North, then south, then all the way north again: the longest possible route, with the final bouquet wilting in the sun. Every order arrived, but next time you will plan the route before setting out.
South and then farther south, in a straight line down the avenue: the most efficient route available. Every order arrived, and you are back at the shop before the florist expects you.
South first, then the long walk back north to 1608. Every order arrived, but your arms ache, and tomorrow you will sort the basket by house number before you leave.

keepsake.title: A Flower Round
keepsake.text: A made-up florist's slip for one spring morning on Prairie Avenue in 1904: which way you went first, and where the last bunch went. No real order, florist or delivery runner is written on it.

evidence.text: Frances Macbeth Glessner kept a journal from 1879 for forty years; in 1904 she set up a silversmith's workbench in the basement of the house; she kept bees; and she held the Monday Morning Reading Class in the library from 1893.
evidence.locator: The biography of Frances Macbeth Glessner.

evidence.text: John and Frances Glessner lived in the house from 1 December 1887 until their deaths (1936 and 1932).
evidence.locator: HABS data pages pp. 1-2 and 9, as data/residents_1904/households/hh_glessner_john_j.json carries them.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book's Prairie Avenue list prints the Blewett Lee household at 1700.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., printed pp. 186-187 (PDF pp. 188-189), as the Prairie library's civic dossier reads it (chicago/prairie_1904_v1/research/civic-dossier.json).

evidence.text: 1700 and 1706 Prairie were twin townhouses John and Frances Glessner built for their two married children; the daughter Frances, married to Blewett Lee in February 1898, moved into 1700 within a few years. George Glessner photographed the pair under construction in 1901.
evidence.locator: The family page's biography of Frances Glessner Lee; the blog's 1901 construction photograph and caption.

evidence.text: Frances Glessner Lee's later work in legal medicine: the Nutshell Studies of Unexplained Death, miniature crime scenes still used in training.

evidence.text: The Clarence Buckingham of the 1904 listing is the Clarence Buckingham (1854-1913) the fountain honours.
evidence.reasoning: The Blue Book lists a Clarence Buckingham in the E. Buckingham household of 2036 Prairie; the fountain honours a Chicago philanthropist and businessman of that name living in 1904 (1854-1913). Same name, same city, same years; no source read here states the identity in words.

evidence.text: The flower runner the visitor plays, their age and work for a florist, the basket and its four orders, the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Flower Round keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such florist, order or delivery is recorded; no named person is met or speaks, and no interior is entered.
